items.title: Beyond Correctness: How Novice Software Engineering Students Exercise Oversight of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is shifting software engineering students' work from producing artefacts towards evaluating and supervising AI-generated outputs. However, little is known about what characteristics students identify in outputs when reporting interventions, or how they exercise oversight during authentic software engineering work. We analysed 962 student-AI interaction turns documented by 145 first-year software engineering students through structured AI Journals, including 172 student-declared interventions. Using a multi-dimensional coding framework, we characterised the output characteristics identified in these reported interventions, students' reasons for intervening, the actions they took, and how those actions were enacted. Fitness problems were identified in 74.4% of interventions, compared with 16.9% involving correctness problems, indicating that oversight more often concerned whether plausible AI outputs were suitable for the engineering task than whether they contained explicit errors. Among classifiable interventions, students most frequently modified generated outputs (51.0%) or refined their prompts (28.2%), with both response types commonly associated with engineering fit. Within-student analysis further showed that outputs perceived as containing minor flaws were associated with lower evaluation confidence than outputs perceived as perfect. Taken together, these findings characterise novice AI oversight as a process that extends beyond error detection to encompass both judgement of fitness for purpose and active intervention in AI-assisted engineering work.

items.title: Beyond Coverage and Mutation: A Blind-Spot Analysis of LLM-Generated Unit Tests
items.abstract: Existing evaluation protocols for unit tests rely on aggregate metrics such as branch coverage and mutation score. These metrics quantify the extent to which a test suite exercises program behavior, but do not identify the behavioral obligations it systematically leaves unchecked. We propose BlindSpotEval, an obligation-based evaluation framework aligned with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. The framework comprises three metrics, Boundary-Value Adequacy, Control-Flow Adequacy, and Oracle Strength, complemented by an assessment of execution reliability. We also introduce ObligBench, a complexity-stratified Java benchmark comprising 895 complex and 700 low-complexity functions with source-side obligation annotations. Evaluating 14,320 tests from four LLMs under four prompting strategies reveals systematic blind spots. Incorrect assertions account for 15.6% of test failures, illustrating that coverage alone does not establish oracle correctness. Among executable tests, coverage of null, negative, and empty arguments reaches only 34.8%, 23.8%, and 38.8%, compared with average coverage above 93% for booleans. Catch blocks and default groups have Control-Flow Adequacy scores of only 0.100 and 0.312. Across both dimensions, LLM-generated tests exhibit the happy-path bias observed in human-written tests, concentrating on normal inputs and expected flows while leaving unusual values and exceptional paths unchecked. Oracle strength is high on average but uneven, with weaker assertions for object return property values and exceptions. These blind spots also occur in low-complexity functions, suggesting that code complexity alone does not explain them. BlindSpotEval provides construct-level adequacy profiles that identify under-tested obligation types and can guide targeted improvements beyond those supported by aggregate scores alone.

items.title: Beyond Data Schedule: Fast LLM Pretraining on Data Mixtures by Loss-Reweighting
items.abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.

items.title: Beyond Gain: Measuring Skill Internalization for Agent Skill Retirement
items.abstract: LLM agents retrieve skills from public hubs that hold up to about 100,000 entries and serve many models. As models improve, a hub must find the skills a given model has internalized, meaning it can do without them, and retire them for that model, yet internalization has not been measured with known reliability. Published rules that compare runs with and without a skill retire on the gain alone. The gain is near zero both for an internalized skill and when neither the model nor the skill delivers the capability, a state we call uncovered. We instead withhold the skill, score the model on a task synthesized from it, and trust a high unaided score only when another model gains from the skill, since nearly half of high scores come from tasks no model benefits from. Under four models, a published gain rule applied with one task per skill removes over half of the uncovered skills. On SkillsBench, 28 of its 31 retirements rest on probes no run passed in full, while retiring on the unaided score costs no detectable reward. Unaided verdicts reproduce across tasks more often than the gain rule's (Cohen's kappa 0.42 against 0.23) but differ across models, so a hub must read them per model. We release 1,251 skills with tasks and item scores under four models.

items.title: Beyond question and answer: Practical applications of multimodal and multifunctional large language models in ophthalmology with a scoping review and future directions
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) connect language understanding with image-based reasoning and are increasingly explored as artificial intelligence systems for ophthalmic image analysis, workflow support, research prototyping, and education. This scoping review synthesizes 21 peer-reviewed studies that moved beyond text-only question answering to evaluate visual question answering (VQA), domain-adapted or fine-tuned ophthalmic models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and low- or no-code tools for analytics and prototype development. Across studies, the evidence suggests early feasibility for image-conditioned explanations, triage support, documentation assistance, structured data extraction, and rapid tool creation. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous and preliminary, with mixed diagnostic performance, variable prompts and model versions, limited external validation, and persistent risks including reasoning errors, hallucinations, session variability, privacy concerns, and security threats. To illustrate potential workflows not yet fully covered by the literature, we also provide clearly labeled author-built demonstrations, which are non-evidentiary, for fundus and optical coherence tomography (OCT)-based VQA, optical character recognition (OCR) tabulation, code-free analytics, automated software programming, and web-based risk calculators. Future priorities include extending image-conditioned reasoning to additional ophthalmic modalities, strengthening RAG with curated corpora and provenance, evaluating few-shot and in-context learning for rare conditions, and using controlled generative imaging for education and data augmentation. Overall, MLLMs may support supervised ophthalmic artificial intelligence applications in selected clinical, research, and educational workflows. Clinical deployment will require external validation, prospective human-in-the-loop evaluation, standards-based workflow integration, privacy-preserving infrastructure, audit logging, cybersecurity, and post-deployment monitoring.

items.title: BEYOND TECHNOSTRESS AI Fatigue as a Cumulative Adaptation Burden in Education and Work
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become a persistent layer of work and learning rather than an occasional tool. Users must repeatedly decide when to delegate, how to prompt, whether to trust, how to verify, and how responsibility should be distributed. This integrative review defines AI fatigue as a cumulative reduction in the cognitive, affective, or motivational capacity for adaptive AI engagement when interaction, evaluation, correction, learning, and role-adjustment demands accumulate faster than recovery and support. The review connects technostress, automation vigilance, cognitive load and offloading, trust calibration, digital fatigue, and the Job Demands–Resources perspective. It introduces an Exposure–Adaptation–Depletion–Response framework, a five-domain taxonomy, and an AI Fatigue Load model that separates use volume from uncertainty, task stakes, correction burden, interruption, role disruption, and imposed adoption velocity. The analysis is updated to incorporate a 2026 validated 15-item AI Fatigue Scale; the proposed load model complements that psychophysiological outcome measure by specifying socio-technical antecedents and exposure conditions. Educational and organizational applications show why AI may simultaneously improve output and worsen human sustainability. The article identifies recurring inferential errors, presents a measurement and longitudinal research agenda, and proposes an intervention hierarchy spanning interface design, workflow, curriculum, organizational policy, and governance. AI fatigue is positioned neither as generic screen tiredness nor as a synonym for burnout, but as an adaptation problem located in the coupled human–AI–institution system.

items.title: BEYOND THE CLASSROOM: ANALYZING THE FACTORS AFFECTING GRADE 12 LEARNERS’ COLLEGE COURSE PREFERENCES
items.abstract: This study utilized a quantitative descriptive-survey and correlational-predictive research design to systematically examine the variables dictating the college preferences of graduating senior high school learners. Conducted at Mindanao State University - Lanao National College of Arts and Trades (MSU-LNCAT) during the School Year 2025–2026, the investigation relied on a total seventy-three Grade 12 learner-respondents comprising of forty-three Humanities and Social Sciences Learner-respondents (58.90%) and thirty TVL track learner-respondents (41.10%), with a demographic concentration of fifty-six females (76.71%) and seventeen males (23.29%). Data was gathered via face-to-face classroom administration using a structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire evaluating three predictive dimensions: Intrinsic Motivation, Familial Influence, and Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence. Descriptive and inferential statistical treatments was used including frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, item ranking, and the Pearson (r) Correlation Coefficient. Intrinsic Motivation emerged as the primary driver, yielding a high composite mean of 3.92 (High Influence) and a Significant Strong Positive Relationship, with course preferences, successfully rejecting the null hypothesis. Conversely, external factors had minimal impact; Familial Influence acted strictly as a secondary, consultative reference point with a neutral composite mean of 3.39 (Moderate Influence) and a weak, variable correlation, while Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence exerted the weakest pressure, finishing with a low composite mean of 2.68 (Low Influence) and No Significant Relationship. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that modern Grade 12 learner-respondents at MSU-LNCAT exercise high psychological autonomy, systematically prioritizing internal passion and specialized tracking competencies over parental expectations, peer circles, or digital trends.

items.title: Beyond What to Say: Proactive Utterance Timing with Inner Thoughts for Werewolf Agents
items.abstract: Participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also whether to speak at all. This judgment carries even greater significance in environments like the Werewolf game, where participants' interests conflict, because both utterances and silence are subject to interpretation and assessment by others. Therefore, determining when to speak, as well as what to say, is crucial for an LLM agent playing the Werewolf game. In this study, we introduce a Werewolf AI agent developed for the Anytime Utterance Track of the AIWolfDial shared task. Our system builds on the existing Inner Thoughts framework, which determines utterance timing during conversations by generating internal thoughts and evaluating the value of each thought for expression at that moment. Since existing methods were designed for general dialogue, we have redesigned the system specifically for the competitive environment and incomplete information setting of Werewolf games. We call our adapted method Adversarial Inner Thoughts. Through experiments involving analysis of self-play logs and human evaluations, we analyze and discuss the effectiveness of our approach.

items.abstract: Big Data and artificial intelligence are changing digital marketing through consumer behavior analysis, personalized communication, and automation. This paper examines their role in marketing processes, performance measurement, and the conditions for application in Serbia. A narrative review of selected literature is combined with a descriptive analysis of published statistics on ICT use, e-commerce, and enterprise AI adoption. The analysis identifies widespread consumer participation in digital channels alongside more limited enterprise adoption of AI. Serbia remains below the EU average in enterprise AI use, although above some member states. The paper’s contribution lies in linking data resources, analytical capabilities, and managerial competencies to explain why technology adoption alone is insufficient for effective digital marketing. Practical implications emphasize employee development, responsible data management, and the evaluation of marketing outcomes. The findings should be interpreted within the limits of aggregate indicators, which do not directly measure marketing-specific AI use or its effectiveness. Future research should examine these applications and their outcomes at the enterprise level.

items.title: Bounding Queue Waits for Fair Scheduling of Bursty HPC Workloads via Hierarchical Algorithms
items.abstract: HPC clusters are shared among many projects, each holding an allocation of node-hours, and ensuring fairness is becoming harder. Foundation models workflows and automated pipelines have made job submissions bursty and concentrated among a few heavy users, so occasional users absorb queueing delays created by frequent ones, with no indication of how long their jobs will wait. Existing schedulers either forget past usage, protect only the job at the head of the queue, or assume that running jobs can be preempted. We propose HyDRA, a Hybrid Deadline and Ranking-Aware scheduler that enforces fairness among users while bounding the queue wait of every job. HyDRA assigns each job a deadline on arrival based on its size, the priorities of its project and user, the current backlog, and how far its project and user are from their entitled share. It ranks waiting jobs by a priority score that grows with waiting time, serves jobs close to their deadlines first, and backfills a job only when no deadline, or fairness limit is violated. We evaluate HyDRA on workloads derived from a year of ALCF Polaris job traces, against conventional schedulers and variants inspired by PCS, Themis, and the PBS job-sort formula used at ALCF. HyDRA achieves $2\times$ the project-level Jain's fairness of the best baseline, starts 47\% of jobs by their deadlines compared with at most 36\% for the baselines even for largest workloads, and lowers the 95th-\%ile bounded slowdown by 4.2$\times$ relative to the next best baseline, at a moderate cost in utilization.

items.title: Building Permit Automatability: A Multi-Level Analysis of Thuringia
items.abstract: The automation of administrative decision-making is increasingly important in digital building permitting. Yet research mainly addresses technically formalisable requirements and rarely examines automation potential across administrative workflows and legal decision situations. This study analyses the Thuringian building permitting process in Germany through a multi-level, process-oriented framework covering planning law, building regulations, procedural rules, and administrative procedure law. The workflow was decomposed into seven modules and 163 decision sub-steps, classified as deterministic algorithm-based, LLM-supported, or non-automatable. Results show marked differences across procedural stages and regulatory layers. Formal and procedural checks offer comparatively high automation potential, whereas planning assessments, inter-agency coordination, and discretionary decisions remain dependent on contextual interpretation and human judgement. Indeterminate legal concepts, discretionary powers, and procedural dependencies are key constraints. The findings support hybrid human-machine approaches rather than full automation.

items.title: Can AI Agents Help Robotic Engineers? Lessons from Two Focus Days in Industry
items.abstract: Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own. However, it is unclear if and how this transfers to robotic engineering, where engineers program industrial robots in niche, vendor-specific languages and rely on visual feedback from simulation tools. Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots. Our results show that the agent did not make the engineers more productive, with the exception of a task that required the generation of highly repetitive code. However, the results with the agent improved over time, as the engineers learned how to use it and the agent was adapted to the domain. Moreover, the experience with AI mattered more for the success with the agent than the experience with robotic engineering. This shows that AI agents are not a plug-and-play solution. Instead, companies must train their engineers on the usage of agents, plan time for a learning curve, and ensure that agent configurations match the domain and developer requirements. The strong learning curve we observed further implies that studies on productivity gains with AI should be longitudinal, as they otherwise miss how engineers adopt agents in practice.

items.title: Can education set the agenda for AI? Simulated innovation and pedagogical direction-setting in teacher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates a critical inflection point in the relationship between educational innovation and technological development. For decades, educational systems have often been positioned reactively: technologies emerge, institutions search for their possible pedagogical uses, and teacher education programmes adapt belatedly to tools designed elsewhere. This article argues that GenAI makes this sequence increasingly insufficient. Because GenAI can produce texts, explanations, feedback, learning resources, and assessment artefacts that resemble evidence of educational performance, it compels education to define more clearly what should count as learning, authorship, judgement, and valid evidence. The article develops the concept of simulated innovation to describe technology-led change that signals modernisation without transforming pedagogical purposes, assessment logics, teacher judgement, student agency, or learning relationships. It then argues that GenAI opens the possibility of pedagogical direction-setting: beginning from educational, ethical, epistemic, and democratic aims, and requiring technology to respond to those aims. Teacher education is positioned as a strategic site for this shift, not because teachers alone can govern AI-mediated education, but because professional formation can prepare educators to translate pedagogical purposes into criteria for design, assessment, ethical judgement, and technology governance.

items.title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
items.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.

items.title: CASE: Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution for Frozen Multimodal Emotion Models
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) by enabling fine-grained emotion understanding through reasoning over multimodal evidence. However, they still exhibit systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with highly overlapping multimodal cues. Existing approaches typically address these errors through global parameter adaptation, making confusion correction costly and inflexible. We instead observe that emotion confusion is highly localized and therefore better addressed through reusable pair-specific expertise. Building on this insight, we propose Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution (CASE), the first agent-skill framework for MER. CASE maintains a sparse, self-evolving library of pair-specific EmotionSkills that externalize affective expertise from model parameters, enabling the learned expertise to be continuously refined and readily transferred across diverse frozen MLLM backbones. During inference, CASE dynamically retrieves the appropriate EmotionSkill to reinforce boundary-aware reasoning while keeping the MLLM backbone frozen. Extensive experiments on CA-MER, DFEW, and EMER demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of CASE across both general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLMs. Notably, CASE improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B on the CA-MER benchmark from 46.80% to 59.13%, while achieving consistent gains across MLLMs.

items.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.

items.title: CEMIR vs. FISER: a comparative study of reasoning-based and enrichment-based approaches to pragmatic intent recognition
items.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.

items.title: Challenges and opportunities in using digital health technologies for decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations in Norway: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Norway has a well-established emergency care system and prehospital infrastructure. However, an ageing population and the increasing prevalence of chronic diseases create a growing need to explore how digital health technologies may support decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations. While technologies such as telehealth, remote monitoring, wearables, portable medical devices, communication platforms, and Artificial Intelligence-based decision-support systems have shown promise for supporting prehospital decision-making, their implementation in Norway remains limited. This study explored Norwegian paramedics’ perceptions of the challenges and opportunities of using digital health technologies to support decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations. Methods An exploratory qualitative interview study was conducted to investigate paramedics’ experiences and perceptions of digital health technology use in decision-making during prehospital non-emergency situations in Norway. Data were collected through 12 semi-structured interviews with paramedics involved in Norwegian ambulance care. Participants were recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework. NVivo 15 and Microsoft Excel were used to support data organization and analysis. Results Four themes captured challenges and opportunities of digital health technologies in prehospital non-emergency situations: digital support for call assessment and ambulance resource allocation; digital patient information for shared situational awareness; digital communication for interprofessional consultation and care coordination; and digital diagnostics for conveyance and non-conveyance decisions. Participants reported fragmented information systems, restricted access to patient records, limitations in communication technologies, and insufficient diagnostic support. They identified opportunities involving video-supported assessment, interoperable patient information, real-time clinical data sharing, multiparty consultation, and point-of-care diagnostics. However, the perceived value of these technologies depended on their reliability, usability, and integration with professional roles and healthcare services. Conclusions Digital health technologies were perceived as having the potential to support decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations by reducing uncertainty and supporting appropriate care pathways. Their perceived value depended on reliable information, interoperability, usable communication, diagnostic support, and clear cross-service responsibilities. Digital transformation should therefore prioritise integrated, context-sensitive systems that augment paramedics’ professional judgement and may enable timely, coordinated, and patient-centred care while remaining responsive to evolving clinical needs and care environments.

items.title: Changes in the acceptance of artificial intelligence in medicine among physicians and the general public in Japan: A repeated cross-sectional comparison of 2018 and 2025
items.abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly, yet whether growing societal familiarity with AI is accompanied by greater willingness to receive relatively autonomous AI-led care remains unclear. We conducted repeated cross-sectional online surveys in Japan in 2018 and 2025 using the same questionnaire and compared self-identified physicians and members of the general public (2018: 399 physicians and 600 members of the public; 2025: 300 physicians and 300 members of the public). Mean responses to the item assessing intention to use medical AI did not differ significantly between survey years in either group, despite consistently favorable evaluations of its usefulness and future necessity. Among physicians, the unadjusted mean response regarding the potential of medical AI to improve clinical efficiency was higher in 2025, but this difference was not significant after adjustment for age and sex. Among members of the public, self-rated knowledge of medical AI was higher in 2025, while expectations that medical AI would increase healthcare costs were also greater. These findings suggest that increased self-rated knowledge may not necessarily be accompanied by greater intention to use relatively autonomous medical AI. Implementation strategies should therefore address concerns regarding responsibility, safety, data protection, and healthcare costs alongside efforts to improve public understanding.

items.title: ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning in the era of generative AI: A bibliometric analysis of research trends, collaboration networks, and emerging pedagogical themes
items.abstract: Purpose – This study aims to map the development of research on ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning during the 2023–2025 period. Methodology – This study uses bibliometric analysis to examine the intellectual, social, and conceptual structures of research on ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning. Data were obtained from the Scopus database and analyzed using Bibliometrix Biblioshiny. Document selection followed the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines as a checklist for the identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion stages. Of the 1,227 documents identified, 143 met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed further. Findings – The number of publications increased from 12 in 2023 to 36 in 2024 and 95 in 2025, indicating an annual growth rate of 181.37% and an average of 18.63 citations per document. International co-authorship accounted for only 16.78% of these documents, indicating limited cross-national collaboration. ChatGPT, mathematics education, and artificial intelligence were the most dominant keywords, while geometry, prospective mathematics teachers, and personalized learning were relatively underrepresented. Novelty – Unlike previous studies that generally treat ChatGPT as part of generative artificial intelligence, this research analytically positions ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning as a separate bibliometric unit and proposes AI-mediated mathematics learning as a conceptual proposition that emphasizes critical validation of AI-generated results. Significance – These findings provide an evidence-based research agenda to strengthen international collaboration and develop mathematics instruction that emphasizes reasoning, justification, and critical evaluation of AI-generated solutions, while identifying priorities for future empirical research.

items.title: Climate Change and Workers’ Health and Safety: An Umbrella Review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesizes current evidence on the health and safety impacts of climate change among workers. In particular, it aims to identify the main workers' categories at the highest risk, the main health and safety outcomes, methodological limitations, and future directions reported in the literature, as well as preventive strategies described in recent reviews. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Systematic and scoping reviews addressing climate-related occupational health and safety outcomes were included. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Methodological quality was assessed using the ROBIS tool, and findings were synthesized in accordance with PRISMA and PRIOR guidelines. RESULTS: Most of the available evidence concerns outdoor occupations, particularly agriculture and construction, where exposure to high temperatures is associated with increased risks of injuries and heat strain. Emerging data also highlight links with mental health, renal disease, and chronic conditions. However, the literature remains fragmented, with few meta-analyses and substantial heterogeneity. Preventive strategies have been proposed, but their implementation remains inconsistent. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence confirms that climate change has become a determinant of occupational health and safety. Future research should strengthen methodological coherence, adopt longitudinal approaches, and address vulnerable populations.

items.title: Comparative evaluation of machine learning algorithms for Maize Lethal Necrosis Disease detection under class imbalance
items.abstract: Maize Lethal Necrosis Disease (MLND) remains a major threat to maize production in sub-Saharan Africa, creating a need for accurate, interpretable, and computationally efficient diagnostic tools. This study presents a comprehensive comparative evaluation of nine machine learning algorithms for MLND detection using a structured feature-based dataset comprising 7,892 maize leaf observations obtained from the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO). The extracted features captured color, texture, lesion, and morphological characteristics associated with MLND symptoms. To address moderate class imbalance, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and class weighting were incorporated within the model development pipeline, and their contribution was quantified through an ablation study. Model performance was evaluated using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation, an independent 80/20 test set, and leave-one-county-out cross-validation (LOCO-CV) to assess geographic generalisability. Across repeated cross-validation, the leading models demonstrated consistent predictive performance with narrow 95% confidence intervals. CatBoost achieved the highest mean accuracy (0.753; 95% CI: 0.730–0.773), while Logistic Regression attained the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC = 0.808; 95% CI: 0.787–0.830). The overlapping confidence intervals among the best-performing models indicate broadly comparable predictive performance, highlighting the importance of considering complementary criteria beyond accuracy alone. LOCO-CV demonstrated minimal performance variation across counties, indicating good internal geographic generalisability. Calibration analysis using Expected Calibration Error (ECE) showed that post-hoc probability calibration substantially improved the reliability of predicted probabilities. At the same time, explainable artificial intelligence techniques consistently identified Chlorosis Intensity, Green–Yellow Ratio, and Necrotic Area as the most influential predictors. Considering predictive performance alongside computational efficiency, model size, and inference latency, LightGBM provided the most favorable balance for resource-constrained environments. In contrast, Logistic Regression offered a highly interpretable alternative with minimal computational requirements. Although the achieved performance indicates that approximately one in four samples may be misclassified and further external validation is required before operational deployment, the findings demonstrate that structured feature-based machine learning provides a transparent, computationally efficient, and interpretable framework for MLND detection and establishes a strong foundation for future field-based decision-support systems.

items.title: Complexity concentration as a god-class and god-method detector: a pre-registered test of a scale-free outlier rule against tool definitions and human labels
items.abstract: God-class and god-method detectors mark concentrated complexity with a raw-scale threshold, a constant fitted on a corpus and re-fitted when the population moves. This paper pre-registers a test of a rule with no raw-scale constant: a unit is a god unit when its complexity is a robust outlier for its own codebase, a modified z-score of 3.5 or more. On 445 repositories in ten languages, 171 of them Java, and the 492 Java repositories of MLCQ, the rule is scored against PMD's GodClass, MLCQ's reviewers and two further definitions, with signal and cutoff chosen on half the repositories and read on the rest. LLM-written code may gather its complexity differently, the case for a detector that needs no re-fitting; the first question is whether one can match the scale of existing human-written code. The verdict is inconclusive on both populations, by different arms. The rule ranks PMD's god classes from the per-file maximum of cognitive complexity at per-repository AUCs of 0.916 and 0.908. On the main run it is, at its default, non-inferior within the margin to a cutoff tuned on the same population on recovery, and flags about twice as many non-god classes; on MLCQ it flags about as many and falls short of the margin on pooled recovery. Pooled, the raw value ranks god classes better than the per-repository score, and a cutoff carried between the populations lost almost nothing: both are human-written code on one scale, so the test is of matching that scale, not of surviving a shift. The rule's extra flags are small classes, just over half holding a method at PMD's own method-level threshold; its misses are large classes whose complexity is spread over many methods. Two readers of the source did not agree on what the extra flags are. Concentration finds where the complexity is; whether that place is a god unit is a question about coupling, which a registered follow-on study takes up. The archive holds the paper (main.pdf) and the arXiv submission bundle (arxiv.tar.gz): the LaTeX source, every generated table and figure, and under anc/ the data the paper is computed from, with a README keying every file to the public repository and command that produces it. The pre-registered plan is tag plan-v1 of the harness repository.

items.title: Computational Peptide Design: Emerging Concepts in Antibiotics, Immunity, and Evolution
items.abstract: Peptides are among the smallest functional biomolecules. Learning to systematically design their activity would revolutionize biology and medicine. Yet achieving this goal remains an open challenge. Recent advances in machine learning enable the discovery and design of peptides at scale, not only yielding new antibiotic agents effective against priority pathogens but also revealing unexpected roles for peptides in host immunity. In this review, we survey how artificial intelligence (AI) methods can be used to mine genomes, proteomes, and even ancient sequence data to uncover “encrypted” peptide antibiotics across the tree of life and over evolutionary time. We highlight emerging approaches for activity prediction, structure–activity modeling, sequence optimization, and de novo peptide generation, and we discuss workflows that tightly couple in silico design with high-throughput experimental validation. We further introduce the concept of “encrypted immunity,” in which ordinary proteins encode latent antimicrobial fragments, and we outline translational opportunities as well as remaining challenges on the path to bringing AI-designed peptides to the clinic.

items.title: Constrained LLM-Guided Model Selection for Cross-Chemistry Early-Life Battery Prognostics
items.abstract: Data-driven battery prognostics can fail when models trained on one chemistry are deployed on another. This study investigates early-life end-of-life (EOL) classification under chemistry-driven domain shift and introduces a schema-constrained large language model (LLM) configuration layer as the primary methodological contribution. The LLM does not predict EOL directly and does not introduce a new transfer-learning or uncertainty-estimation algorithm. Instead, it maps structured chemistry context and numerical dataset evidence to an executable architecture, reliability head, and bounded set of training hyperparameters selected from an approved model zoo containing one-dimensional CNN, self-attention, WideResNet, OpenMax, and Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP) options. Full degradation trajectories define five EOL categories using an 80% state-of-health threshold, whereas model inputs are restricted to early-cycle observations. items.title: Constructing a Generative AI Framework for Personalised Instructional Resource Development: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation in a Micro-Lecture Design and Production Course
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is promoted as a way of tailoring instruction to learners, yet most reported applications stay within language and general-education settings, and few measure outcomes in courses whose value lies in design and production skill. This paper describes a four-module generative AI framework for resource development that links learner and content modelling, generation, assessment and community iteration to a course-grounded knowledge base, with the teacher reviewing before release. It was evaluated in a twelve-week quasi-experiment in a professional core course, Micro-lecture Design and Production, at a Chinese vocational college. Two intact classes (n = 45, 44) were taught by the same instructor, who designed the framework; assignment was not random. Covariance-adjusted posttest means differed by 5.6 points (82.3 versus 76.7, p < .001, partial η² = .24), and the framework-supported class reported higher motivation and satisfaction; self-directed learning differed modestly. Preparation time per unit fell by half, though the work became more concentrated and the knowledge base carried a large one-off cost. Because the design cannot separate the framework from the additional resources it produced, the results are framed as associations rather than effects.

items.title: Constructivist Learning in Indonesian Islamic Boarding Schools: A Critical Discourse Analysis of English Lesson Plans
items.abstract: Jean Piaget’s constructivist theory emphasizes active knowledge construction, yet its application in Indonesian Islamic Boarding Schools (IIBS) remains limited. This phenomenological case study examines how constructivist principles are integrated into IIBS English lesson plans using a critical discourse analysis approach. Seven lesson plans from an IIBS in East Java were analyzed over six months. Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis (CDA) was employed to examine power dynamics and ideological influences in classroom discourse within the lesson plans. Findings revealed that while constructivist elements such as problem-based learning, collaborative discussions, and metacognitive reflection are present, their implementation is constrained by hierarchical teacher-student relationships and religious-nationalist discourse framing. Lesson plans encourage active engagement but often reinforce predefined moral and ideological narratives, limiting opportunities for critical inquiry and independent knowledge construction. Despite this, Piagetian principles align with certain Islamic educational traditions, such as ijtihad (independent reasoning) and shura (consultative learning), providing potential avenues for deeper cognitive engagement. This study empirically contributes to qualitative evidence on how Piaget’s constructivist theory is applied within IIBS. This study also offers a practical hybrid pedagogical approach that combines experiential learning with structured guidance, fostering critical thinking without disrupting Islamic traditions.

items.title: Controlled Evaluation of EEG Foundation Models: Random Initialisation, Band-Power and Validation-Selected Probes
items.abstract: EEG foundation models report downstream gains, yet their protocols seldom include three controls. These are the same encoder untrained, spectral features fitted on the same data, and a layer picked without looking at test scores. We therefore evaluate five publicly released EEG foundation models and an in-house JEPA-style model under one protocol with all three controls and several seeds, on five benchmarks and four added task families. The controls change the reading in three ways. First, picking the probed layer by its test score raises the layer-wise peak by an average of +0.034 and reverses the peak-versus-output gap in 9 of 36 cells. Second, with the layer picked on validation, random initialisation matches or beats pretraining for half of the models on sleep and emotion, and no model beats a five-band log-power baseline on emotion or motor imagery. Third, after full fine-tuning only 5 of 30 pairs gain beyond twice their seed spread, and the one clear loss of -0.290 AUROC persists under matched learning rates. From these results we draw four reporting practices, and we release every cell for re-analysis.

items.title: Conversational AI in Digital Marketing: Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty
items.abstract: This study examined associations among Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty in the use of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for Indonesian e-commerce. A cross-sectional survey collected questionnaire responses from 300 purposively selected consumers who had experience with e-commerce chatbots or virtual assistants. The analysis used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 to assess 18 indicators across three reflective constructs. The reported measurement properties met the specified reliability and validity thresholds. The reported PLS-SEM results indicated positive direct associations among Human-Like Interaction, Perceived Empathy, and Customer Loyalty, alongside a positive specific indirect association through Perceived Empathy. However, discrepancies between the structural model and the direct-effects table prevent a definitive interpretation of the estimated effect magnitudes and mediation type. However, coefficients in the structural diagram differed from those in the direct-effects table, so the magnitudes and type of mediation could not be confirmed from the reported outputs. The study distinguishes perceived conversational naturalness from perceived understanding and company-directed loyalty intentions. These findings concern self-reported perceptions and intentions rather than observed repurchase behavior. Its cross-sectional design and purposive sample preclude causal conclusions and population-wide generalization. The results provide a basis for evaluating interaction quality and perceived understanding in chatbot-supported customer service.

items.title: Crowd Discrimination in the Digital Workplace: How AI and Platforms Translate Public Bias into Employment Practices
items.abstract: In today's digital workplace, employment decisions are increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI) and social media platforms, embedding societal biases into managerial practices and undermining traditional legal safeguards. This article introduces the concept of crowd discrimination, which arises when biases originating from customers, algorithms, or online communities influence employment outcomes, thus threatening workers' right to equality. Specifically, it argues that platform-based work, AI-driven management tools, and online shaming systematically transform crowd biases into employment decisions regarding hiring, dismissal, wages, and working conditions. Crowd discrimination is not incidental. It results from both technological design and the limitations of existing laws, which fail to adequately address these new discriminatory practices. Employers utilize AI and platform infrastructures, whether intentionally or not, to distance their decisions from discriminatory effects, thereby evading legal accountability. Meanwhile, platform and AI companies shape employment conditions through their technologies without recognized legal responsibility, complicating employers' obligations under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and obscuring the sources of discrimination. To address these challenges, the article calls for new legal duties to protect workplace equality. It proposes procedural protections enabling workers to enforce equality rights, particularly in cases mediated by AI systems and platforms. Further, it argues for imposing direct liability on platform and AI companies whose technologies facilitate discrimination, whether through embedding biased patterns into AI tools or allowing customer preferences to dictate employment outcomes. By adopting this broader legal approach, the article offers a comprehensive framework to address the threats crowd discrimination poses to workplace equality.

items.title: Damage-TriageFormer: A foundation-model framework for typology-based building damage assessment from mono-temporal imagery
items.abstract: Decision-relevant building damage assessment is critical for prioritizing resources and recovery after a disaster. Most automated methods, however, either flatten damage into a single severity scale (no damage, minor, major, destroyed) or require paired pre- and post-event imagery that is often unavailable for emerging hazards. This paper presents Damage-TriageFormer, a single-image, post-event, footprint-conditioned model that produces a damage typology rather than a severity scale. We make two contributions. First, DamageTriage-Bench combines NOAA Emergency Response Imagery from Hurricane Michael (2018), Hurricane Helene (2024), and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfire complex with five typology classes that distinguish roof from structural damage and partial from total extent. Its photo-atomic splits keep all tiles from a source photo in one fold. Second, Damage-TriageFormer pairs a DINOv3 ViT-L backbone with a two-stage gated damage head and an auxiliary severity objective under building-footprint conditioning. Across three training seeds, its crop-conditioned configuration reaches mean macro F1 of 0.662 on validation and 0.620 on the held-out test fold. Controlled experiments associate this performance with the crop training recipe as a whole, which differs from the recipe of the tile-level variant in the trainable layers, learning rates, logit adjustment, weight averaging, and schedule: training the same crops with the tile-level recipe lowers test macro F1 by 0.067, whereas the head variants and the effective input resolution of the crops show no statistically distinguishable differences. The model is most accurate on the two visually distinct endpoint classes, with mean test F1 of 0.92 on undamaged buildings and 0.85 on total structural collapse. The aggregate expected calibration error of the seed-42 checkpoint is 0.016, but class-conditional analysis shows that its rare-class predictions are overconfident. While the rare Total Roof Damage class remains difficult, consistent with its limited examples and an ambiguous label boundary, the results show that single-image post-event imagery contains useful signal for building damage typing without a pre-event reference. Field use would still require external validation, reliable footprint data, and human inspection.

items.title: Data Analytics in Management Accounting: A Bibliometric Analysis
items.abstract: This study examines the evolution of research on data analytics in management accounting by identifying publication trends, influential contributors, collaboration networks, and emerging research themes. Using bibliometric methods, including performance analysis and science mapping, the study analyzes 129 articles published in Scopus-indexed journals between 2014 and 2025. The findings show that the literature is primarily centered on accounting information systems, big data, and artificial intelligence, while machine learning, blockchain technology, and cloud computing have emerged as significant directions for future investigation. By mapping the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of this research domain, the study provides a comprehensive overview of existing knowledge, identifies key research gaps, and proposes an integrative agenda for future research. These findings offer useful insights for both researchers and practitioners seeking to advance the application of data analytics in management accounting.

items.title: Data availability and FAIRness in intervention studies on oral mucositis in children and adolescents: a meta-research study
items.abstract: This meta-research study will assess the availability and FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of data supporting the primary outcomes of intervention studies on oral mucositis in children and adolescents (0–19 years). Oral mucositis is a painful and common complication of chemotherapy, head and neck radiotherapy, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation conditioning. It can affect eating, speaking, infection risk, and cancer treatment itself. Data sharing in dentistry has been shown to be rare, but no study has yet assessed it in pediatric oral mucositis research specifically. We will run a systematic search, with no language or date restrictions, of MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses. We will include prospective intervention studies, randomized or non-randomized, in which at least one primary outcome relates to oral mucositis. Screening, data extraction, and all assessments will be performed independently by one human reviewer and a generative AI tool (Claude, Anthropic) acting as second reviewer, with disagreements resolved by a third human reviewer. For each study, we will classify both declared and effective data availability, including the data availability statement, access route, repository, identifier, license, and documentation. When data are "available on request," we will contact the authors in a standardized way. We will assess located datasets that have a persistent identifier or resolvable URL using the automated F-UJI tool. Risk of bias (RoB 2 / ROBINS-I) and discrepancies between registered and reported primary outcomes will be explored as secondary aims. The study will not synthesize clinical effects. We expect to estimate the proportion of studies with complete, partial, or no effective data availability and to describe the FAIRness levels of the datasets we locate, including differences between publication periods (up to 2015 vs. 2016 onward). The findings should show where data transparency and responsible reuse can be improved in pediatric oral mucositis research.

items.abstract: Abstract: Title: L0 Invariant State Matrix (L0-ISM): A Deterministic Control Architecture for Critical L0 Infrastructure and Boundary-Constrained Systems Abstract:The increasing reliance on probabilistic Artificial Intelligence and continuous floating-point algorithms in Operational Technology (OT) and Level 0 (L0) critical infrastructure introduces unacceptable risks of stochastic drift, computational latency, and unpredictable edge-case failures. Drawing from the historical transition from additive, zero-less Roman numerals to positional Arabic numerals, this paper argues that modern AI suffers from a structural "Roman Matrix Bloat"—attempting to solve physical control problems by infinitely scaling parameter spaces rather than anchoring value to position and structural equilibrium. To eliminate unconstrained floating-point infinities, we introduce the **L0 Invariant State Matrix (L0-ISM)** architecture—a fundamentally deterministic control paradigm based on discrete positional geometry and axiomatic teleology. The L0-ISM framework maps multidimensional physical and operational parameters onto a rigid, symmetric discrete scale ranging from -9 to +9 using unique, non-repeating positional digits (from 0 to 9), where 0 represents absolute thermodynamic or logical equilibrium (the fulcrum of a balance scale). System states are encapsulated as finite k-dimensional tuples and routed through precompiled Lookup Tables operating in constant time O(1), entirely eliminating computational latency and stochastic uncertainty. The architecture features hardware-level absorbing boundaries at -9 and +9 for immediate interdiction (Hard Stop, -999) and integrates input hysteresis alongside temporal gradients to ensure physical stability against signal noise and actuator chatter. items.title: DealsFlow: An Evidence-Gated Agentic Harness for Venture Capital Deal Triage
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can read startup pitch decks, but letting them emit investment scores directly invites score inflation, run-to-run variance and rationales that are hard to audit. We describe DealsFlow, a human-in-the-loop agentic harness deployed at a UK early-stage fund. The LLM reads the deck, cites evidence and rates each category; code combines the ratings, caps them and only ever lowers them. Three mechanisms implement this: a stage-aware corroboration ceiling (78, 70 or 60 out of 100) on factual categories without external evidence; a sceptic call that may lower but never raise a score; and a pre-fetch pattern that retrieves and indexes all evidence before a single generation pass. We evaluate on $N=243$ SEIS/EIS investments with recorded outcomes. Because recent investments have unresolved outcomes, we use the 142 that are at least three years old. There, the full pipeline's score has Spearman $ρ=0.45$ (95% CI 0.32 to 0.57) with the total-value multiple and AUC 0.71 for identifying write-offs, against $ρ=0.38$ and AUC 0.68 for an unconstrained LLM. The gain is small and comes mostly from the sceptic call; we did not test whether its lower-only rule matters. Investments that later exceeded $2\times$ had 64% of factual categories corroborated, against 38% for write-offs (omnibus Kruskal-Wallis test over five outcome groups, $p=0.031$), and our retrieval was not date-restricted, so these figures may overstate screening skill. In a study of 20 inbound applications, analyst time per application fell from 44.7 to 18.9 minutes including verification and correction, and 84% of 240 cited claims were fully supported by their sources, but 70% of reports needed at least one correction.

items.abstract: This whitepaper analyzes the structural problem of centralization in the development of modern artificial intelligence and proposes a conceptual model of decentralized training based on blockchain technology. It examines how the concentration of data, computational infrastructure and models in a reduced number of global corporations creates technological, economic and strategic dependency worldwide. Through progressive examples—from the basic workings of machine learning to the reuse of computations through hashes—the idea of a distributed network (IAChain) is introduced, in which nodes, data, storage and trainings coexist incentivized through digital tokens. The goal is not to present a finished technical solution, but to open a discussion about the feasibility and potential impact of decentralizing the knowledge and processing that will sustain the next generation of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Decolonising Generative AI in South African Teacher Education: Wayfinding for Multilingual, Indigenous, and Publicly Accountable Futures
items.abstract: Abstract This viewpoint article argues that South African teacher education requires a distinctly decolonial agenda for generative artificial intelligence (AI), developed in critical dialogue with scholarship from Aotearoa New Zealand and wider international contexts. AI is not a neutral efficiency tool: its infrastructures, training data, evaluation standards, and platform logics can intensify linguistic hierarchy, data extraction, epistemic marginalisation, and pedagogical standardisation. Drawing on epistemic justice, decoloniality, settler-colonial analysis, and wayfinding, the article synthesises policy and scholarship to develop a framework for multilingual, Indigenous, and publicly accountable AI in teacher education. The comparison is deliberately relational rather than transfer-oriented. South Africa and Aotearoa have distinct colonial histories, constitutional arrangements, and Indigenous political formations; nevertheless, Te Tiriti o Waitangi-informed educational thinking, Māori data and algorithmic sovereignty, and Pacific-led teacher education provide productive tests of whether AI governance redistributes authority or merely adds cultural content to externally controlled systems. The article advances six interdependent propositions: language justice by design; Indigenous Knowledge Systems stewardship; critical AI literacy for teacher agency; assessment redesign around process and judgment; public-interest data governance; and infrastructure-aware inclusion. Decolonising AI, it concludes, is not metaphorical branding or the insertion of local examples into imported systems. It requires material changes to curriculum purposes, decision rights, data relations, evaluation criteria, and institutional accountability so that AI strengthens multilingual participation, community authority, teacher judgment, and public benefit.

items.title: Deep Learning-Based Fruit and Vegetable Quality Grading Using Computer Vision: Recent Advances, Challenges, and Future Directions:Review
items.abstract: The grading of fruits and vegetables is mostly dependent on subjective visual inspection techniques that require labor. Computers and advanced machine learning systems can help to invent non-destructive tools for quality evaluation of fruits and vegetables based on color, size, shape, texture, ripeness, freshness, and surface damage based on computer vision methods. The paper is presenting reviews of methods used for fruit and vegetable grading, including convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, object detection systems, vision transformers, hyperspectral and multimodal vision techniques, and few-shot learning approaches. The review focuses on grading effectiveness, computation complexity, data variety, and algorithms reliability, and it shows that although many studies report the accuracy level higher than 99% while working with particular datasets, most studies used private datasets, making the comparison of results between various studies impossible. In this regard, the paper addresses the issue of a gap between benchmarks and real-life deployment and proposes a framework based on the grading process that includes a confidence lock mechanism for uncertain predictions and a reliable protocol for testing and benchmarking performances of the algorithms This paper lacks any experimental data as the proposed framework and procedures are designed for future assessment.

items.title: Deep Learning: A Taxonomy and Research Roadmap
items.abstract: This technical report presents a structured taxonomy and research roadmap for deep learning, distinguishing among neural architectures, computational mechanisms, learning paradigms, task-specific architectures, and complete AI systems. The report surveys foundational neural networks, convolutional neural networks, recurrent and sequence-to-sequence architectures, attention mechanisms, Transformer architectures, vision Transformers, generative models, graph deep learning, state-space models, neural differential equations, and deep reinforcement learning. It further examines self-supervised and multimodal learning, mixture-of-experts architectures, meta-learning, continual learning, federated learning, computer vision systems, speech and audio models, time-series modeling, recommendation architectures, metric learning, domain adaptation, knowledge distillation, causal deep learning, neuro-symbolic AI, and emerging neural architectures. The report also covers training and optimization methods, normalization and regularization, large language model efficiency, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, model compression, efficient inference, LLM training and alignment, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic AI, and foundation-model systems. Each major method family is organized around milestone tables, mathematical formulations, and descriptions of its historical development. The report concludes with an overview of the evolution of deep learning, research-oriented mastery levels, and a structured research pathway for natural language processing and large language models. items.title: Democratizing LLM Training with the Edge: Challenges, Systems, and the Road Ahead
items.abstract: The growing computational power of modern GPU data centers has let a few industrial giants train and deploy large language models (LLMs) on massive amounts of data. Yet the sheer scale of these models and their training data makes centralized development increasingly hard to sustain, and at the same time shuts out smaller institutions that hold relevant private data but lack comparable infrastructure. In this paper, we organize our positions on distributed LLM training around the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms, covering federated learning, split learning, and decentralized approaches, and we assess their readiness for geo-distributed settings with heterogeneous hardware and unreliable connectivity. We then present a {\em unified} system architecture built around a cloud-hosted parameter server that coordinates heterogeneous clients over outbound gRPC connections, reusing one communication, compression, and fault-tolerance stack for both pretraining and a family of fine-tuning methods. We validate the design with real geo-distributed experiments on GPT-2 Medium and Llama3-1B pretraining across multiple university sites, showing stable convergence under realistic conditions. Finally, we chart the road ahead, identifying open problems that span frontier model support, elastic fault tolerance, adaptive compression, federated alignment, privacy and trust, incentive design, and system--algorithm co-design, all of which must be addressed to make democratized LLM training a reality.

items.title: Design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience models for mitigating phishing and social engineering attacks in the U.S. banking sector: A data paper with a synthetic benchmark dataset
items.abstract: Phishing and social engineering remain the main routes to fraud against bank customers. Static warnings lose force as users habituate to them. This paper presents APUX-Bank. This paper is a synthetic benchmark for the design and evaluation of adaptive AI-based user experience (UX) models that defend bank customers against phishing. The dataset simulates a four-arm randomized experiment with 2,400 U.S. adult bank customers and 28,800 message decisions across email, SMS, voice and in-app channels. The four arms are a static warning, a rule-based adaptive warning, an AI-adaptive warning and an AI-adaptive warning with an explanation (AI-XAI). The data were generated from a seeded hierarchical logistic model. Its parameters were set from published phishing research. Logistic regression with participant-clustered errors showed that the AI-adaptive design reduced the odds of clicking a phishing message by 48 percent (OR = 0.52, 95% CI [0.45, 0.59]). The AI-XAI design reduced the odds by 56 percent (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.39, 0.51]). The benefit was largest for customers with low digital literacy. AI-XAI also raised usability by 6.2 points on the System Usability Scale and lowered false alarms. Trust in the system mediated 41 percent of its effect on phishing reports. The results held across GEE, random-intercept, probit and linear probability models. A parameter recovery test found that 29 of 31 true values fell inside their 95 percent confidence intervals. The data and all Python code are released for teaching, power analysis and method testing Keywords: Phishing, Social Engineering, Adaptive User Experience, Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Banking Security, Synthetic Data, Logistic Regression.

items.title: Design and evaluation of augmented reality head-up displays for driving: A multivocal review of interaction challenges, research gaps, and future directions
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to provide an integrated synthesis of recent research and practice on the design and evaluation of Augmented Reality Head-Up Displays (AR-HUDs), with particular emphasis on interaction challenges, design and evaluation strategies, and unresolved research challenges. A Multivocal Literature Review (MLR) was conducted to address the fragmented coverage of these dimensions in previous reviews and to systematically integrate academic and practitioner-oriented evidence. Studies published between 2020 and January 2026 were identified from academic databases and grey literature sources, resulting in a final evidence pool of 110 studies, comprising 97 white-literature and 13 grey-literature sources. The findings showed that cognitive and visual perception challenges were the most frequently reported interaction issues, while design and evaluation practices exhibited substantial methodological heterogeneity and inconsistent operationalization of key human-factor constructs. The integration of white and grey literature revealed complementary perspectives, with academic studies predominantly providing empirical evidence on driver interaction and human factors, while practitioner-oriented sources complemented this evidence with implementation, validation, and emerging technological considerations. The synthesis further identified information management, spatial and optical configuration, evaluation standardization, real-world assessment, and adaptive and context-aware interfaces as important research directions. These findings provided an evidence-informed basis for linking interaction challenges with design and evaluation practices and for guiding more human-centered, systematically evaluated, and practically grounded AR-HUD development.

items.abstract: Abstract Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is commonly associated with cognitive impairments and psychosocial difficulties that significantly affect quality of life beyond seizure burden. Individuals with DRE frequently experience difficulties in attention, memory, executive functioning, emotional regulation, stress, stigma, and social participation. Despite the high prevalence of these comorbidities, integrated rehabilitation approaches addressing both neurocognitive and psychosocial domains remain limited, particularly in resource-limited clinical settings. This article aims to develop and evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of a structured neurocognitive and psychosocial intervention module for individuals with DRE. A multidisciplinary intervention module integrating psychoeducation, cognitive retraining exercises, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and family counseling was developed through literature review, clinical observations, and expert feedback. The intervention was delivered in eight weekly group sessions in Hindi and English at a tertiary neurology center in India. Ten adults with DRE participated in the pilot study. Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, retention, attendance, adherence to home-based activities, and participant engagement. Acceptability was assessed through structured participant feedback regarding clarity, usefulness, relevance, and overall satisfaction with the intervention. Nine of 10 participants completed the intervention. Attendance, engagement, and adherence to home-based activities were satisfactory among participants who completed the study. Participants reported that the intervention content was understandable, relevant, and useful in daily functioning. Cognitive retraining exercises and CBT sessions were perceived as beneficial for improving coping, emotional regulation, and cognitive engagement. Family counseling sessions were positively received and were considered helpful in improving caregiver understanding and family support. One participant reported anxiety related to task performance during cognitive exercises. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of a structured neurocognitive and psychosocial intervention module for individuals with DRE within a tertiary care clinical setting. Further randomized controlled studies are underway to evaluate the clinical efficacy and long-term applicability of the intervention.

items.title: Designing of specialized language model for medical diagnosis: a systematic review of architectures, applications, and clinical challenges
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large Language Models have become impactful in medicine by facilitating the processing of difficult medical data and aiding diagnosis-making. Given general LLM’s weaknesses, specialized medical LLMs are constructed for clinical precision, contextual understanding and safety in risky diagnostic applications. This review summarizes recent trends in medical LLMs for diagnosis, reported during 2021–2025. Methods A systematic literature review was performed following the PRISMA methodology. A search was designed and systematically carried out in the SCOPUS database using criteria of inclusion and exclusion (type of publication, language, period and country) and 75 peer-reviewed articles were chosen from a database of 1,911 records, after a multi-stage screening and eligibility evaluation. Results In summary, there have been significant advancements in the design and application of medical LLMs, with trends in hybrid architecture, multi-modal learning, prompt optimization techniques, diffusion-based imaging models, and multi-agent diagnostic system models. However, a number of persistent challenges that need to be overcome remain in the development and implementation of these models; namely, hallucination, bias, and poor probability calibration in LLMs, issues with explainability of LLMs, and ineffectiveness in a clinical environment. Conclusions This review highlights the fast pace of development and limitations of domain-specific medical LLMs. While impressive improvements in diagnostic performance have been made, the future directions must address improvements in reliability, safety and clinical validation in order to be seamlessly and responsibly incorporated in the practice.

items.title: Designing sustainable urban intelligence: a green AI framework and survey
items.abstract: The accelerating pace of urbanization has intensified demands on energy, water, transportation, and waste management systems, necessitating intelligent solutions that are both effective and environmentally sustainable. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has demonstrated significant potential in optimizing urban operations; however, the increasing computational complexity and energy consumption of AI models pose new sustainability challenges. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Green AI methodologies and introduces the Green AI Urban Framework (GAUF), a structured conceptual framework for integrating environmentally responsible AI into sustainable urban systems. The survey examines recent advances in energy-efficient model design, lightweight and adaptive learning techniques, data-efficient training, and resource-aware deployment strategies. Major urban application domains, including electricity demand prediction, water resource optimization, waste management, and smart mobility, are analyzed to identify current capabilities, limitations, and research gaps. Building on these insights, GAUF integrates three core components: sustainability-aware model selection, cloud–edge deployment strategies, and energy-efficiency evaluation metrics across the AI lifecycle. The framework also incorporates implementation and governance considerations relevant to urban infrastructure, sustainability reporting, and municipal adoption. GAUF aims to support researchers, practitioners, and policymakers in designing AI-driven urban systems that balance predictive performance, scalability, and environmental responsibility. By consolidating existing research and outlining future research directions, this study contributes to the development of sustainable AI practices as a core component of next-generation smart and resilient cities.
